title: One hundred thousand appends of 640-character values into a flow sequence that the patch itself created, a 64 MB result, with a hang guard that a pass over the whole collection for every operation exceeds
notes: The patch first adds an empty sequence `f` and then copies a 640-character string from `/v` onto `/f/-` 100,000 times, each time appending one item. It is the shape of `safety/patch-many-appends-into-a-created-flow-sequence` at a much larger size: that case has to stay in the fast set, so its expected bytes are a stored file of under a megabyte and it uses 240-character items and 4,000 operations. The result here is 64.2 MB, and its expected bytes and its patch are built from recipes (docs/case-format.md). Each operation is valid and changes one place, so the work that the patch needs is linear in the size of the result: the time a library needs must not depend on how many operations came before. The append goes at the end of the sequence and only `]` and a line break follow it, so no library has a reason to touch more than the new item. A library that rescans, re-parses or copies the whole flow collection for every operation does work for each operation that grows with the collection, so its total time grows with the square of the number of operations: here 100,000 passes over a collection that grows to 64 MB, about 3.2 trillion bytes. The time limit is 80 seconds and is a hang guard, not a measure of cost. The size is chosen so that the guard still has force: a model reader that allocates, copies and frees the collection once per operation, at 13 GB/s, needs 250 seconds, and one that walks it at 5 GB/s needs 640 seconds. A library whose work for each operation grows with the number of items rather than with the bytes of the collection does far less work than that model and can still finish inside the guard: two libraries measured on this case take about 20 seconds at 100,000 operations and about 4 seconds at 50,000, so their cost grows with the square of the number of operations and the guard does not catch it at this size. The only results allowed are the exact bytes below or a limit error: a limit on the number of operations or on the size of the result is not wrong. The copy is from a value of the input and not an inline string because 100,000 inline strings of this size would make a patch of 64 MB. The bytes rest on two kit conventions: a new member goes at the end of its mapping and items of a flow sequence are separated by `, `, so the case carries the tag `convention`. The case carries the tag `slow` because its expected result is larger than a megabyte. Output: `a: 1`, `v: ` and the 640-character string, then `f: [` and 100,000 copies of the string separated by `, `, then `]`. The time bound is the robustness requirement of the kit, not a rule of the specification.

provenance.reference: A patch engine whose cost per operation grew with the size of the flow collection it appended to, so a long patch took quadratic time; found in the Go library with items longer than the smaller sibling case could state.
